shevuot-26a-16-17.note: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi were standing before their teacher Rav after a lesson and disagreed about what he had said. Each swore an oath that Rav had said it his way. When they asked Rav, he agreed with one of them. The other asked, "Did I then take a false oath?" Rav answered, "Your heart compelled you."
shevuot-26a-16-17.why: A teaching about oaths says that someone forced by circumstances beyond his control is not liable to bring an offering for a broken oath. The Gemara asks what such circumstances look like, and answers with this case of a man who swore sincerely but was mistaken.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A student of Rav who swore an oath about what Rav had said.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: A student of Rav who swore the opposite oath about what Rav had said.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Their teacher, who settled what he had said and reassured the one who had sworn wrongly.

terms.meaning: A solemn statement made in God's name. Swearing falsely is a serious sin, and in some cases the one who did it must bring an offering at the Temple to atone.

shevuot-30b-3-3.note: The wife of Rav Huna had a case before the judge Rav Nahman. He was caught in a bind: if he stood up for her, as the wife of a Torah scholar deserves, the other side might feel he favored her and hold back their claims; if he did not stand, he would fail to honor her. So he told his attendant to go outside, make a duck fly up and throw it at him, so that he would have to stand up anyway.
shevuot-30b-3-3.why: The Gemara is discussing who must stand and who may sit in court, and the Torah scholar's dignity in a trial. Right after this, it asks how Rav Nahman could stand at all when judges should sit while giving a verdict.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge hearing the case, who found a way to stand for the woman without seeming biased.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Torah scholar; his wife was a litigant in the case.

terms.meaning: Literally a 'fellow': someone devoted to careful observance of the commandments. The principle quoted is that the wife of a haver is honored as he is.
One of the two sides in a court case.

shevuot-30b-6-6.note: Rav bar Sherevya, a Torah scholar, had a case before Rav Pappa against an ordinary unlearned man. Rav Pappa seated them both. A court officer came, kicked the unlearned man and made him stand up, and Rav Pappa did not tell him to sit down again. The Gemara asks how he could allow it, since the man might now feel too intimidated to press his claims. Rav Pappa reasoned that the man would think: the judge seated me; it is only the officer who has it in for me.
shevuot-30b-6-6.why: Rabba bar Rav Huna has just ruled that when a scholar and an unlearned man go to court, both are told to sit, and if the unlearned man stands out of respect that is no problem. This case shows the ruling in practice.

people.name: Rav bar Sherevya
people.about: A Torah scholar who had a court case before Rav Pappa.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The judge, who seated both sides and let the officer's action stand.

terms.meaning: Literally 'people of the land': an ordinary person without Torah learning, as opposed to a Torah scholar.
A court officer who carried out the judges' orders and kept order in the courtroom.

shevuot-32b-4-5.note: A man snatched a silver ingot from another. The victim came before Rabbi Ami, with Rabbi Abba sitting there, and brought one witness who saw the snatching. The accused said, "Yes, I snatched it, but I snatched what was mine." Rabbi Ami was stuck: one witness is not enough to make him pay, but he cannot be let off either, and having admitted to snatching he counts as a robber who cannot be trusted to swear. Rabbi Abba answered that he is someone who must take an oath but cannot, and such a person pays.
shevuot-32b-4-5.why: The Gemara is asking when a single witness who falsely denies what he knows is liable for a false oath of testimony. Abaye says all agree in a case like this one, because here one witness's testimony would make the defendant pay.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The judge before whom the case came.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: A Sage sitting with Rabbi Ami, who gave the ruling that settled the case.

terms.meaning: Jewish law needs two witnesses to make someone pay. A single witness cannot do that, but he can force the defendant to swear an oath denying the claim.

terms.term: obligated to take an oath but unable to
terms.meaning: A rule that someone who must swear to clear himself, but is not allowed to swear (for example because he is presumed a thief), has to pay instead.

shevuot-34a-17-18.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Shatah swore that he had seen a man chase another into a ruin. He ran after them and found the man with a sword in his hand, blood dripping, and the victim in his death throes. He said, "Wicked one, who killed this man? Either I did or you did. But what can I do? Your blood is not in my hands, since the Torah requires two witnesses to put a man to death. The Omnipresent will exact payment from you." The Sages said they had not moved from there before a snake bit the killer and he died.
shevuot-34a-17-18.why: Rav Pappa is asking whether testimony based on knowledge without seeing the act can exist in capital cases. Rabbi Aha holds that circumstantial evidence counts, and this case is the example of knowing a man killed without seeing it.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: The Sage who saw the aftermath of the killing and tells the story under oath.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written code of Jewish law.
A name for God, meaning the One who is everywhere.

terms.term: I will not see the consolation
terms.meaning: A form of oath: may I not live to see the comfort and redemption of Israel if what I say is untrue.

shevuot-34b-2-2.note: A man told another, "I lent you a hundred dinars beside this column." The other answered, "I never passed beside this column." Two witnesses came and said they had seen him urinate beside that very column. Reish Lakish ruled that he is now presumed to be a man who denies the truth.
shevuot-34b-2-2.why: Just before, Rav Yehuda asked whether witnesses who saw money being counted out from outside can testify about the loan. The Gemara brings a similar case of witnesses who undercut a denial, and Rav Nahman then rejects Reish Lakish's ruling as fit only for a Persian court.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: The Sage who ruled that the man who denied passing the column is presumed a liar.

terms.meaning: A silver coin; a hundred dinars was a sizable loan.
Once a person is shown to have lied in a case, the court no longer believes his claims in that case.

shevuot-34b-4-4.note: In another version of the case, a man told another, "I lent you a hundred dinars beside this column." The other answered, "I never in my life passed beside this column." Witnesses came and said they had seen him urinate beside that column. Rav Nahman ruled that he is now presumed to be a man who denies the truth.
shevuot-34b-4-4.why: In the first version Rav Nahman objected because the man only denied passing the column in connection with the loan. Here he said "never," so Rav Nahman accepts the ruling; Rava then objects that people do not remember things they have no reason to.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: In this version, the Sage who ruled that the man is presumed a liar.

terms.meaning: Once a person is shown to have lied in a case, the court no longer believes his claims in that case.

shevuot-41b-8-11.note: A lender told a borrower: when you repay me, do it in front of two people who have learned halakha. The borrower repaid him privately, with no one present, and the coins were then taken by forces beyond the lender's control. The lender came before Rav Naḥman: yes, I took the money, but only as a deposit to hold until two learned people came along and the condition could be met, so the loss is not mine. Rav Naḥman said that since he admitted taking it, it was a full repayment. And if he wanted the condition met, let him bring the money now, since Rav Naḥman and Rav Sheshet had learned halakha, Sifra, Sifrei, Tosefta and the whole Talmud.
shevuot-41b-8-11.why: The Gemara is collecting cases about repaying loans before witnesses. Just before, Rava ruled that a lender who names particular witnesses can insist on them; here Rav Naḥman holds that money the lender admits receiving is repaid regardless.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Judge who held that the debt had been repaid.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: Sage named by Rav Naḥman as fully learned, along with himself.

terms.meaning: Jewish law.
Early collections of the Sages' teachings, studied alongside the Mishna.
Property held for safekeeping. An unpaid keeper is not liable when it is lost through forces beyond his control.

shevuot-41b-14-14.note: A man told another, "Give me the six hundred dinars you owe me." The other answered, "Didn't I pay you with a hundred kav of gallnuts worth six dinars a kav?" The lender replied, "Weren't they worth only four a kav?" Two witnesses came and said yes, they were worth four. Rava ruled that the borrower is now presumed to be a man who denies the truth. Rami bar Hama objected that Rava himself had said people forget things they have no reason to remember. Rava answered that people do remember the market price.
shevuot-41b-14-14.why: This is one of a series of cases about when a debtor caught in a false claim loses credibility. Rava has just said a debtor wrongly naming witnesses to a repayment may simply have forgotten; this case shows where he draws the line.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled that the borrower is presumed a liar.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: A Sage who challenged Rava with his own earlier ruling.

terms.meaning: A measure of volume used for dry goods.
Round growths on oak trees, used for tanning leather and making ink, and traded as a commodity.
Once a person is shown to have lied in a case, the court no longer believes his claims in that case.

shevuot-42a-6-6.note: A borrower told his lender, "I will believe you any time you tell me I have not repaid you." He then went and repaid the debt in front of witnesses, and the lender later said he had not been paid. Abaye and Rava both said the lender is believed, since the borrower had agreed to trust him. Rav Pappa objected: he trusted him more than himself, but did he trust him more than witnesses?
shevuot-42a-6-6.why: The Gemara has been discussing when a lender's claim that a payment went to some other debt is believed. This case turns to a borrower who gave his lender advance credibility, and the next cases test how far such a promise reaches.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who, with Rava, ruled that the lender is believed.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who, with Abaye, ruled that the lender is believed.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Sage who objected that the borrower never meant to trust the lender over witnesses.

shevuot-42a-6-9.note: A borrower told his lender: whenever you say I have not repaid, I will believe you as if you were two witnesses. He then repaid the loan in front of three witnesses. Rav Pappa ruled that the lender could not deny it: the borrower had trusted him like two witnesses, not like three. Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, objected that following the larger number applies to estimates of value, where more people know more, but in testimony a hundred witnesses are like two and two are like a hundred.
shevuot-42a-6-9.why: The Gemara has just argued over a borrower who makes his lender believable against any claim of repayment, and whether that trust can outweigh witnesses; this case asks whether the number of witnesses changes the answer.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who rules that trust 'like two witnesses' does not stand against three.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: The Sage who objects that in testimony the number of witnesses beyond two makes no difference.

terms.meaning: The rule that when people disagree, the view held by more of them is accepted. Rav Huna says it fits estimates of value, not testimony.

shevuot-47a-7-9.note: A man snatched a piece of metal from another. The victim came before Rav Ami, with Rabbi Abba sitting there, and brought one witness who saw the snatching. The accused said, "Yes, I snatched it, but I snatched what was mine." Rabbi Ami asked how to judge it: one witness is not enough to make him pay, he cannot be let off since there is a witness, and he cannot be told to swear because by admitting the snatching he counts as a robber. Rabbi Abba answered that he is someone who must take an oath but cannot, and such a person pays.
shevuot-47a-7-9.why: The Gemara is asking what Rabbi Yosei meant when he said that an oath nobody can take "returns to its place." Rav Pappa says the Sages of the Land of Israel meant Rabbi Abba, and this case shows Rabbi Abba holding that the defendant who cannot swear must pay.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The judge before whom the case came (called Rav Ami at first in the English).

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: A Sage sitting with Rabbi Ami, who gave the ruling that settled the case.

terms.meaning: Jewish law needs two witnesses to make someone pay. A single witness cannot do that, but he can force the defendant to swear an oath denying the claim.

terms.term: obligated to take an oath but unable to
terms.meaning: A rule that someone who must swear to clear himself, but is not allowed to swear (for example because he is presumed a thief), has to pay instead.
